tracks.narration: The ground is perfectly flat here, yet it is neither a hilltop nor the bottom of a valley.
Take the surface z equals x squared minus y squared. At the origin the gradient is zero, so it is a critical point — but the surface curves up along one axis and down along the other.

Spin a cutting plane through the centre. Along one direction the slice is a valley that curves upward; rotate by ninety degrees and it becomes a ridge that curves downward; halfway between, the slice is perfectly flat.
Opposite curvature in the two principal directions means the Hesse eigenvalues have opposite signs, and the discriminant is negative. That is the signature of a saddle.
A saddle point is a minimum one way and a maximum the other — so a zero gradient alone never guarantees an extremum.
